cards.text: Last chapter of Leviticus, friend, and the LORD has more to say to Moses. He tells Moses to speak to the Israelites about this: what happens when someone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value of persons.

Then comes a whole price list in silver, set by age and by male or female, from one month old all the way to sixty and older. Top of the list is a man from twenty to sixty at fifty shekels, and friend, I came with a price sticker that said 25 CENTS.

cards.question: Now somebody makes that vow, but they're too poor to pay the price on the list. What happens?

answers.text: The priest sets a price they can afford
The vow is canceled at no cost
A neighbor pays the full price for them

cards.text: Next up: animals. Somebody vows an animal that may be brought as an offering to the LORD.

cards.question: An animal fit to be brought as an offering is vowed to the LORD. What does it become?

answers.text: Free to return to the herd

cards.question: Once an offering animal is vowed to the LORD, the owner may swap it for a better one.
The owner swaps his vowed animal for another one anyway. Which animal ends up holy?

cards.text: Now, what if the vow involves an unclean animal, one that may not be brought as an offering to the LORD? That one gets handled differently.

cards.question: When an unclean animal is vowed, the ___ sets its value, whether high or low.
The owner decides he wants to buy back the unclean animal he vowed. What must he do?

answers.text: Add a fifth to its value

cards.text: Now a man consecrates his whole HOUSE as holy to the LORD, and the priest values it, good or bad. Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer, so a whole house sounds like a castle to me.
And if he wants that house back, he pays the assessed value plus a fifth, and it's his again.

Now land: a man consecrates a parcel of his land to the LORD, and it's valued by the seed it takes, fifty shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed. If he does it during the Year of Jubilee, that price stands.

cards.question: But say the man consecrates his field after the Jubilee. How does the priest figure the price?

answers.text: By the years left until the next Jubilee
By how big last year's harvest was
By what the owner first paid for it

cards.text: Same deal if he wants the field back: add a fifth to the assessed value, and it belongs to him.

cards.question: Now say the man never buys his consecrated field back, or he sells it to another man. Can it be redeemed after that?

answers.text: No it can no longer be redeemed
Yes by adding a fifth to its value
Yes once the Year of Jubilee comes

cards.question: When that field is released in the Jubilee, it becomes holy and belongs to the priests.

cards.text: Now a man consecrates a field he bought, one that isn't part of his own property. The priest figures its value up to the Year of Jubilee, and the man pays it that same day as a sacred offering to the LORD.

cards.question: A man consecrated a field he bought. When the Year of Jubilee comes, where does that field go?

cards.text: Every value uses the sanctuary shekel, twenty gerahs to the shekel. Then comes a firstborn of the livestock, an ox or a sheep, and nobody may consecrate one.

cards.question: Why can't anyone consecrate a firstborn ox or sheep to the LORD?

answers.text: It already belongs to the LORD
It is too young to be offered
It belongs to the oldest son

cards.question: A firstborn that's an unclean animal can be redeemed with a fifth added. If it isn't redeemed, it is ___ according to its value.

cards.text: Now a different word: devoted. A man sets apart something he owns to the LORD, whether a man, an animal or his inherited land, and everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.

cards.question: A man can buy back something he devoted to the LORD by adding a fifth to its value.

cards.text: And no person set apart for destruction may be ransomed. He must surely be put to death.
Last topic, friend: the tithe from the land, whether it comes from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees.

cards.question: The tithe from the land's seed and fruit trees is holy. Who does it belong to?

cards.text: Want to buy back part of your tithe? Add a fifth. Friend, that fifth keeps showing up like crumbs on my apron.

cards.question: Every ___ animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd's rod is holy to the LORD.
While counting the herd, the owner may check whether each tenth animal is good or bad and swap it out.

cards.text: And if he swaps anyway, both animals become holy, and neither one can be redeemed.
These are the commandments the LORD gave Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai. And that, friend, is the last word of Leviticus.

findings.problem: Moses appears for the first time in this lesson, but the card never says who he is. It only says "the LORD has more to say to Moses."

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The question says "Now somebody makes that vow." The word "that" points back to the vow from cards 1 and 2, which are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The question says "When that field is released in the Jubilee." The words "that field" point back to the field from card 4, which is no longer on screen. The question never says which field: a consecrated field that wasn't redeemed or was sold.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Stop 1 has six choice cards: four multiple choice, one true or false and one fill in the blank. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Many story cards are flat restatements of the law with no Papa Dorin voice, for example stop 1 card 12 and stop 2 cards 3, 13 and 19. The whole walkthrough has only three mild jokes (stop 1 cards 2 and 11, stop 2 card 16). None of them reach laugh-out-loud. The stop 1 card 11 joke compares house size, not the act of consecrating the house.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Almost the whole chapter (Lev 27:2-33) is detailed rules for valuing vows, consecrated property, firstborn and tithes. That fits the long-stretch list ("rules for offerings and feasts") and "mostly detail and not much happens." The walkthrough sums up only 27:3-7 as a stretch and goes through the rest item by item, with choice cards, like the bad Exodus 21-23 example. But a stretch "never gets a stop of its own" and must sit with "the moments around it," and here the stretch is nearly the entire passage. There are almost no moments around it.
findings.question: When a whole passage (here, a Sermons-type passage in the Be Holy group) is a long stretch of rules, should Prep sum it up in one or a few story cards with no choice cards? Or do vow and tithe laws count as "teaching and key laws" that get choice cards like the rest of a passage?
